Secrets and lies - nuclear two

By: Joy Summers | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
The biggest deal south Africa has ever done will be concluded by year end but despite questions South Africans are still in the dark

Further information:
CAPE TOWN - Russia's state energy corporation Rosatom on Wednesday denied that it had already secretly won a massive nuclear power contract in South Africa, and sought to allay fears of corruption over the deal.
Critics of the government's controversial plan to build eight nuclear reactors worth up to R1,24 trillion should "stop worrying", Victor Polikarpov, Rosatom's regional vice president, told AFP.
Five nations - Russia, France, China, the United States and South Korea - are competing for the contract, but there is widespread speculation that President Jacob Zuma's close relationship with Russian President Vladimir Putin has sealed the deal for Rosatom.
"This is not true, these are insinuations and rumours," Polikarpov said.
"I don't know (where) they come from -- maybe we were the first to sign an inter-government agreement and it was rather comprehensive compared to similar agreements signed by other countries."
A row erupted in September last year when Rosatom appeared to announce that it had won the nuclear power contract, prompting allegations that Zuma's government had dodged procurement rules.
But Pretoria insisted at the time that the Russia deal simply initiated the procurement phase of the project and that other countries would be given a chance to bid.
The winning bid is expected to be announced by the end of this financial year.
Cost estimates for as many as eight reactors generating 9,600 megawatts, which the government wants to begin operating from 2023 and complete by 2029, range from R460 billion to R1,2 trillion
The fear of possible corruption in the massive upgrade deal is fuelled by accusations of kickbacks involving Zuma and other government officials in a multi-billion-dollar arms deal in 1999.
Polikarpov acknowledged this but said the South African government was taking pains to ensure the procurement process was clean.
"I think that measures taken by the government are directed towards avoiding a similar case with the arms deal.
"They are doing their best -- to comply with the constitution, to make it cost effective, to make it transparent. There will be an international auditing company hired to monitor the assessment of the deal," he said.

Unsafe, unreliable- Vladimir Slivyak’s verdict on Russian nuclear reactors
Reactors from Russia are unsafe and unreliable, India shouldn’t buy them: Russian environmentalist Vladimir Slivyak DiaNuke.org, 9 Jan 15 “………….Over a dozen incidents and failures have already occurred at the newly built VVER at Kalinin NPP, including one involving a hydrogen explosion.
The Russian fast breeder reactor – the only commercial unit of this type in the world – has in its over 30 years of operation experienced almost as many various accidents, including fires involving radioactive substances and coolant leaks.
Further development of the breeder technology planned by Rosatom in Russia includes experiments with plutonium fuel. VVER-1200s are also designed to operate with plutonium fuel. Introducing this nuclear material into electricity generation on an industrial scale will likely lead to new accidents that will result in plutonium contamination.
Additionally, eleven old RBMK units – all variations on the Chernobyl design – still remain in operation in Russia.
Rosatom continues to reprocess spent nuclear fuel at the disastrous Mayak facility. Not only is the stockpile of extracted plutonium growing, but there is also a constant significant increase in volumes of radioactive waste resulting from reprocessing. The Mayak nuclear facility in Chelyabinsk Region was a place of a devastating nuclear accident of 1957, which caused widespread radioactive contamination and led to the resettlement of about 20,000 of local residents in the subsequent years.
Unfortuntely, several thousands of local residents still have to live in contaminated area because Rosatom doesn’t take responsibility for their resettlement and people themselves are too poor to move away. That’s best illustration of what is safety culture and social responsibility in understanding of the Russian nuclear industry.
Russia has no realistic and viable plan for the disposal of radioactive waste. The risk of radioactive leaks from the aging radioactive waste storage facilities is increasing. Rosatom’s attempts to build new disposal sites for radioactive waste in several regions of Russia have been met by harsh opposition from local populations and environmental groups. But even if such sites were ultimately built, their capacity would be enough to take care of only a small fraction of the waste accumulated over many decades.
How strong is the nuclear safety regulation in Russia? What have been post-Fukushima changes?
Unfortunately, it’s far from strong. In 1990s we had special safety regulator, Gosatomnadzor (or GAN). It was reporting directly to the president of country and was able to confront Rosatom on the most important safety issues. I mean there is certain difference in mandates of operator and regulator, and they must be in confrontation to improve the safety. When regulator becomes a friend to operator we are getting into Japanese situation which in the end bring us to another Fukushima sort of disaster. But that’s not the way it went in Russia. Rosatom successfully lobbied for dissolving of independent GAN. And finally it became just the department inside of another bigger structure, without any ability to control. After Fukushima, regulator proposed to close several old reactors down but that was easily ignored by Rosatom who said Russian reactors are best in the world and Fukushima would never happen in Russia. Something like that was said by Western industry after Chernobyl and all wanted to believe in it until Western-designed Fukushima exploded several times.
The Russian nuclear giant, Atomsroyeport, has been clearly unwilling to abide by the Indian liability law which has a clause on supliers liability in case of an accident. What does it say on their claims of safety?
It just confirms old fact that there is no 100% safe reactors. Which means, sooner or later, new Chernobyl or new Fukushima (or both) will happen again somewhere in the world. Russian industry knows very well that their reactors have vulnerabilities. And they don’t want to pay in case of another Chernobyl which they know is possible. Just like the owner of Fukushima is not paying to Japanese people……….http://www.dianuke.org/russian-reactors-are-unsafe-and-unreliable-india-shouldnt-buy-them-russian-environmentalist-vladimir-slivyak/

Press Release:


SA’s Nuclear Future
South Africa’s government is forging ahead with its ambitions to acquire nuclear energy and wants the first reactor online by 2023. While the Department of Energy wants to finalise a strategic partner by the end of the year and has signed framework agreements with the Russians, the Americans, the Chinese, the French and the South Koreans, the programme remains shrouded in secrecy. Is the project viable? And, what is the true cost? Carte Blanche investigates.


Script:


NUKE TWO 27th August 2014 FINAL SCRIPT

Commentary One
Russian Vladimir Slivyak is out here as a consultant to Earth Life Africa. He looks harmless enough on this borrowed bicycle, but the organization he founded in Russia is considered dangerous to the Kremlin. His NGO is now on a list labeled foreign agents

VLADIMIR
Foreign agents at Stalin times, …it were spies and they were all killed so what Putin government does is they introduce the word foreign agent again to make people scared…

Commentary Two
Vladimir is the founder of a Russian environmental NGO called ECODEFENCE. They stopped Rosatom, the Russian nuclear utility from building a reactor by targeting the banks Rosatom hoped would finance it.
The reactor build was stopped

Vladimir
A month after construction was stopped we got on the list

BONGANI
Does that make you an enemy of the state?
Vladimir
You can say like this ja.

Commentary Three
Russia under President Putin has embarked on an aggressive campaign to sell its nuclear reactors.

Vladimir
Once you build nuclear reactors you become dependent on this country pretty much. It’s not business – they are not making money on it, its world influence

Commentary four
Last year South Africa signed amongst others, an inter-governmental framework agreement with Russia. When it was kept secret here, it was Vladimir that leaked the agreement with South Africa

LINK
Journalists have had a tough time trying to extract details about the biggest procurement deal this country has ever seen. What we do know is that behind the scenes – the process is moving extremely quickly

Commentary Five
Gordon Mackay is the DA shadow minister for energy



GORDON
When you consider how long it takes to procure textbooks in this country it is amazing that they want to procure a whole nuclear fleet by the end of this year, which is December 2015

Commentary six
Our requirements are 9600 MW split between 6- 8 reactors at these proposed sites in the Eastern and Western Cape and a proposed new one in KZN.

BONGANI LINK
Our own nuclear ambitions go way beyond the purchase of a few reactors. We want to, not only build reactors, but export them too

Commentary seven
At Pelindaba, NECSA CEO Phumzile Tshelane is one of the high level insiders advising on the programme.

Bongani
There has been much criticism around perceived secrecy and yet even at this stage, I am not sure how this will all work?

Phumzile Tshelane
Its very difficult to understand what I am telling you – I am saying we are going to procure capability – have you ever heard of that concept? That we are procuring capability not equipment, and when you explain this you have to do it over and over again

LINK
I will take that one on the chin. Maybe I am just a simple guy, but I understand money and the projected costs of this programme have differed wildly.

Commentary eight
Last month the energy Department chose the Zimbali Luxury resort to update journalists on the progress of the nuclear build programme, but once again the department revealed little

ZIZAMELE MBAMBO
It is important to note that government is still to negotiate the price tag during the procurement phase which is why we cant make them available to the public at this stage

Commentary nine
At NECSA they were more forthcoming

CEO
Anywhere between 10 billion dollars to 40 billion dollars
Bongani
Some people have speculated that it could cost a trillion rand or more
CEO
Yes I have seen that speculation – I don’t know where that figure comes from

GORDON MACKAY
The department is saying 500 billion but nuclear new build programmes globally are running over 75% in terms of cost – not included in the costs are financing costs which is probably about R250 billion worth – also consider the management of nuclear waste - so when the Government says one trillion is not the amount they are right – it is going to be a lot more than that

Commentary ten
This week Greenpeace activists staged an anti nuclear demonstration outside the Department of Energy. Executive Director Kumi Naidoo

KUMI NAIDOO –International Executive Director
If people think the arms deal is a big deal in terms of corruption, then this will make the arms deal look like a Sunday morning picnic!

Commentary eleven
France, USA, South Korea, China and Russia have signed binding intergovernmental agreements with SA, but these were never discussed in parliament because they were tabled as technical agreements and technical agreements do not have to go for discussion. Yet by December a strategic partner will be presented to Cabinet according to the energy minister

LINK
But then they will have to make it snappy because Government wants the first reactor up and rolling by 2023.

Phumzile Tshelane NECSA
The normal construction period for reactors is five years and now we have eight years to go we certainly can fit a sixty-month period between now and 2023

Commentary twelve
Mycle Schneider is one of the lead authors of the World nuclear industry status report, which is based only on empirical evidence, he told us from Paris.

Bongani
The first reactor is supposed to go on stream in 2023. Is that feasible?

Mycle Schneider
It’s not a matter of optimistic or pessimistic, from PAST data it’s impossible!

Commentary thirteen
His data shows that 40 nuclear reactors started in the last ten years took an average time of 9.4 years to build.




Mycle
Now if we use the term building time, it means from the base matt concreting to grid connection. And you know the lead-time is much longer than that so we are talking about projects that take 15 years at least.

When we look at the Russian industry, amongst those 40, there were three in Russia that started up. Do you know what the average construction time was 28 years! 28 years for three Russian reactors

Bongani
Some critics will say that this is not possible
Phumzile
Well the critics have never built reactors. It is certainly achievable – it’s tight but it’s achievable

Mycle
To give you an order of magnitude – if you look at the three reactors with building times of 28 years – this is about 3000 MW in capacity – the German record of installation of 3000MW is one month of installation!

Commentary fourteen
Despite the denials – indications are that Russian nuclear state company Rosatom is a likely frontrunner in our own bidding process

VLADIMIR
Who is Rosatom?
Vladimir
It’s a big organization working all across the world to serve the political goals of the Kremlin
Bongani
That is the unofficial explanation
Vladimir
Ja

Commentary fifteen
Chernobyl is a black mark on Rosatom’s name, but there have been other smaller accidents too, says Vladimir who is amazed that the framework agreement we signed, excludes all Russian organisations from liability in the event of an accident

Vladimir
It’s clearly stated there that Russian companies will not have any responsibility in case of a nuclear accident or any kind of problem

Commentary sixteen
Rosatom is offering South Africa its generation 3 water pressurized reactors



VLADIMIR
And this new design is not under construction in Russia yet, not in operation anywhere in the world and there is no safety record of course because those reactors don’t exist yet
Bongani
We would be guinea pigs?
Vladimir
Yes that is what Russian Rosatom is trying to make out of here

LINK
We have asked Rosatom for an interview a couple of times. They say not now, but other sources of information on this state owned entity- well they are not very flattering

Commentary seventeen
In October 2014 Greenpeace published an in depth look at the company. It says that Rosatom presents considerable and troubling problems as a potential business partner from finance to performance to significant safety concerns

Kumi Naidoo
What is the problem with business partner Rosatom? One look at their track record does not give confidence, and I think that banking on Rosatom delivering on time is backing the wrong horse.

Bongani
Rosatom the Russian company has said that there is an agreement in place and they believe they have won.

Phumzile Tshelane NECSA
I have seen that in terms of the commentary in newspapers. The important thing is that there is no contract between South Africa and Russia, there is no contract between any company and South Africa to do the nuclear

Commentary eighteen
The French state controlled energy group Areva way behind schedule in Finland, has been downgraded to junk status but Areva say, plans to return the company to strong operational performance are well underway.


MYCLE
Actually people have to understand that AREVA is technically bankrupt so– it would not survive the year so the decision was to have the state utility take over the building from AREVA

Commentary nineteen
The big elephant in the room is how South Africa will fund this programme-
We don’t have the money, the World Bank doesn’t finance nuclear and it may be a stretch even for the BRICS new development bank



NECSA Phumzile Tshelane
If you build a reactor you will generate profit from the reactor, its not as though someone will have the 10 billion dollars sitting somewhere to build all this equipment

Commentary twenty
Russia has funded the Turkish reactor at Akkuyu, but now the Russian economy has tanked, and do we want a business partner like President Putin? He was voted person of the year in 2014 by the Organized Crime and Corruption Reporting Project. Putin, they claim did the most to enable and promote organized criminal activity.

GORDON
If Rosatom is going to be able to finance the deal they will be able to call the shots that is just fundamentally how it works, which in a way means that you are sacrificing elements of your national sovereignty – ANC government saying we must keep Eskom because it’s a national asset, and yet here we are saying lets hand over 9- 10 reactors to a foreign power to operate within our borders

Commentary Twenty-one
In a recent ANC discussion document, a call is made for Government to commit to a full, transparent and thorough cost benefit analysis of nuclear power…and this can only be procured after a proper affordability assessment

Bongani
Mycle if we pursue this this programme despite the warnings what will it mean for South Africa?

Mycle
You have to realize that many projects around the world have never realized – we have identified 92 reactors under construction that have never been put into operation /so it would be a huge waste of money

THE END 12’ 02’’

What we do know is that behind the scenes – the process is moving extremely quickly Commentary Five Gordon Mackay is the DA shadow minister for energy GORDON When you consider how long it takes to procure textbooks in this country it is amazing that they want to procure a whole nuclear fleet by the end of this year, which is December 2015 Commentary six Our requirements are 9600 MW split between 6- 8 reactors at these proposed sites in the Eastern and Western Cape and a proposed new one in KZN. BONGANI LINK Our own nuclear ambitions go way beyond the purchase of a few reactors. We want to, not only build reactors, but export them too Commentary seven At Pelindaba, NECSA CEO Phumzile Tshelane is one of the high level insiders advising on the programme. Bongani There has been much criticism around perceived secrecy and yet even at this stage, I am not sure how this will all work? Phumzile Tshelane Its very difficult to understand what I am telling you – I am saying we are going to procure capability – have you ever heard of that concept? That we are procuring capability not equipment, and when you explain this you have to do it over and over again LINK I will take that one on the chin. Maybe I am just a simple guy, but I understand money and the projected costs of this programme have differed wildly. Commentary eight Last month the energy Department chose the Zimbali Luxury resort to update journalists on the progress of the nuclear build programme, but once again the department revealed little ZIZAMELE MBAMBO It is important to note that government is still to negotiate the price tag during the procurement phase which is why we cant make them available to the public at this stage Commentary nine At NECSA they were more forthcoming CEO Anywhere between 10 billion dollars to 40 billion dollars Bongani Some people have speculated that it could cost a trillion rand or more CEO Yes I have seen that speculation – I don’t know where that figure comes from GORDON MACKAY The department is saying 500 billion but nuclear new build programmes globally are running over 75% in terms of cost – not included in the costs are financing costs which is probably about R250 billion worth – also consider the management of nuclear waste - so when the Government says one trillion is not the amount they are right – it is going to be a lot more than that Commentary ten This week Greenpeace activists staged an anti nuclear demonstration outside the Department of Energy. Executive Director Kumi Naidoo KUMI NAIDOO –International Executive Director If people think the arms deal is a big deal in terms of corruption, then this will make the arms deal look like a Sunday morning picnic! Commentary eleven France, USA, South Korea, China and Russia have signed binding intergovernmental agreements with SA, but these were never discussed in parliament because they were tabled as technical agreements and technical agreements do not have to go for discussion. Yet by December a strategic partner will be presented to Cabinet according to the energy minister LINK But then they will have to make it snappy because Government wants the first reactor up and rolling by 2023. Phumzile Tshelane NECSA The normal construction period for reactors is five years and now we have eight years to go we certainly can fit a sixty-month period between now and 2023 Commentary twelve Mycle Schneider is one of the lead authors of the World nuclear industry status report, which is based only on empirical evidence, he told us from Paris. Bongani The first reactor is supposed to go on stream in 2023. Is that feasible? Mycle Schneider It’s not a matter of optimistic or pessimistic, from PAST data it’s impossible! Commentary thirteen His data shows that 40 nuclear reactors started in the last ten years took an average time of 9.4 years to build. Mycle Now if we use the term building time, it means from the base matt concreting to grid connection. And you know the lead-time is much longer than that so we are talking about projects that take 15 years at least. When we look at the Russian industry, amongst those 40, there were three in Russia that started up. Do you know what the average construction time was 28 years! 28 years for three Russian reactors Bongani Some critics will say that this is not possible Phumzile Well the critics have never built reactors. It is certainly achievable – it’s tight but it’s achievable Mycle To give you an order of magnitude – if you look at the three reactors with building times of 28 years – this is about 3000 MW in capacity – the German record of installation of 3000MW is one month of installation! Commentary fourteen Despite the denials – indications are that Russian nuclear state company Rosatom is a likely frontrunner in our own bidding process VLADIMIR Who is Rosatom? Vladimir It’s a big organization working all across the world to serve the political goals of the Kremlin Bongani That is the unofficial explanation Vladimir Ja Commentary fifteen Chernobyl is a black mark on Rosatom’s name, but there have been other smaller accidents too, says Vladimir who is amazed that the framework agreement we signed, excludes all Russian organisations from liability in the event of an accident Vladimir It’s clearly stated there that Russian companies will not have any responsibility in case of a nuclear accident or any kind of problem Commentary sixteen Rosatom is offering South Africa its generation 3 water pressurized reactors VLADIMIR And this new design is not under construction in Russia yet, not in operation anywhere in the world and there is no safety record of course because those reactors don’t exist yet Bongani We would be guinea pigs? Vladimir Yes that is what Russian Rosatom is trying to make out of here LINK We have asked Rosatom for an interview a couple of times. They say not now, but other sources of information on this state owned entity- well they are not very flattering Commentary seventeen In October 2014 Greenpeace published an in depth look at the company. It says that Rosatom presents considerable and troubling problems as a potential business partner from finance to performance to significant safety concerns Kumi Naidoo What is the problem with business partner Rosatom? One look at their track record does not give confidence, and I think that banking on Rosatom delivering on time is backing the wrong horse. Bongani Rosatom the Russian company has said that there is an agreement in place and they believe they have won. Phumzile Tshelane NECSA I have seen that in terms of the commentary in newspapers. The important thing is that there is no contract between South Africa and Russia, there is no contract between any company and South Africa to do the nuclear Commentary eighteen The French state controlled energy group Areva way behind schedule in Finland, has been downgraded to junk status but Areva say, plans to return the company to strong operational performance are well underway. MYCLE Actually people have to understand that AREVA is technically bankrupt so– it would not survive the year so the decision was to have the state utility take over the building from AREVA Commentary nineteen The big elephant in the room is how South Africa will fund this programme- We don’t have the money, the World Bank doesn’t finance nuclear and it may be a stretch even for the BRICS new development bank NECSA Phumzile Tshelane If you build a reactor you will generate profit from the reactor, its not as though someone will have the 10 billion dollars sitting somewhere to build all this equipment Commentary twenty Russia has funded the Turkish reactor at Akkuyu, but now the Russian economy has tanked, and do we want a business partner like President Putin? He was voted person of the year in 2014 by the Organized Crime and Corruption Reporting Project. Putin, they claim did the most to enable and promote organized criminal activity. GORDON If Rosatom is going to be able to finance the deal they will be able to call the shots that is just fundamentally how it works, which in a way means that you are sacrificing elements of your national sovereignty – ANC government saying we must keep Eskom because it’s a national asset, and yet here we are saying lets hand over 9- 10 reactors to a foreign power to operate within our borders Commentary Twenty-one In a recent ANC discussion document, a call is made for Government to commit to a full, transparent and thorough cost benefit analysis of nuclear power…and this can only be procured after a proper affordability assessment Bongani Mycle if we pursue this this programme despite the warnings what will it mean for South Africa? Mycle You have to realize that many projects around the world have never realized – we have identified 92 reactors under construction that have never been put into operation /so it would be a huge waste of money THE END 12’ 02’’ Invoicing Back references from Insert ID in Invoice: Title Author Last Updated Invoice for Secrets and lies - nuclear two (4606) Joy Summers 29 August 2015

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): The biggest deal south Africa has ever done will be concluded by year end but despite questions South Africans are still in the dark
metadata.Further information: CAPE TOWN - Russia's state energy corporation Rosatom on Wednesday denied that it had already secretly won a massive nuclear power contract in South Africa, and sought to allay fears of corruption over the deal. Critics of the government's controversial plan to build eight nuclear reactors worth up to R1,24 trillion should "stop worrying", Victor Polikarpov, Rosatom's regional vice president, told AFP. Five nations - Russia, France, China, the United States and South Korea - are competing for the contract, but there is widespread speculation that President Jacob Zuma's close relationship with Russian President Vladimir Putin has sealed the deal for Rosatom. "This is not true, these are insinuations and rumours," Polikarpov said. "I don't know (where) they come from -- maybe we were the first to sign an inter-government agreement and it was rather comprehensive compared to similar agreements signed by other countries." A row erupted in September last year when Rosatom appeared to announce that it had won the nuclear power contract, prompting allegations that Zuma's government had dodged procurement rules. But Pretoria insisted at the time that the Russia deal simply initiated the procurement phase of the project and that other countries would be given a chance to bid. The winning bid is expected to be announced by the end of this financial year. Cost estimates for as many as eight reactors generating 9,600 megawatts, which the government wants to begin operating from 2023 and complete by 2029, range from R460 billion to R1,2 trillion The fear of possible corruption in the massive upgrade deal is fuelled by accusations of kickbacks involving Zuma and other government officials in a multi-billion-dollar arms deal in 1999. Polikarpov acknowledged this but said the South African government was taking pains to ensure the procurement process was clean. "I think that measures taken by the government are directed towards avoiding a similar case with the arms deal. "They are doing their best -- to comply with the constitution, to make it cost effective, to make it transparent. There will be an international auditing company hired to monitor the assessment of the deal," he said. Unsafe, unreliable- Vladimir Slivyak’s verdict on Russian nuclear reactors Reactors from Russia are unsafe and unreliable, India shouldn’t buy them: Russian environmentalist Vladimir Slivyak DiaNuke.org, 9 Jan 15 “………….Over a dozen incidents and failures have already occurred at the newly built VVER at Kalinin NPP, including one involving a hydrogen explosion. The Russian fast breeder reactor – the only commercial unit of this type in the world – has in its over 30 years of operation experienced almost as many various accidents, including fires involving radioactive substances and coolant leaks. Further development of the breeder technology planned by Rosatom in Russia includes experiments with plutonium fuel. VVER-1200s are also designed to operate with plutonium fuel. Introducing this nuclear material into electricity generation on an industrial scale will likely lead to new accidents that will result in plutonium contamination. Additionally, eleven old RBMK units – all variations on the Chernobyl design – still remain in operation in Russia. Rosatom continues to reprocess spent nuclear fuel at the disastrous Mayak facility. Not only is the stockpile of extracted plutonium growing, but there is also a constant significant increase in volumes of radioactive waste resulting from reprocessing. The Mayak nuclear facility in Chelyabinsk Region was a place of a devastating nuclear accident of 1957, which caused widespread radioactive contamination and led to the resettlement of about 20,000 of local residents in the subsequent years. Unfortuntely, several thousands of local residents still have to live in contaminated area because Rosatom doesn’t take responsibility for their resettlement and people themselves are too poor to move away. That’s best illustration of what is safety culture and social responsibility in understanding of the Russian nuclear industry. Russia has no realistic and viable plan for the disposal of radioactive waste. The risk of radioactive leaks from the aging radioactive waste storage facilities is increasing. Rosatom’s attempts to build new disposal sites for radioactive waste in several regions of Russia have been met by harsh opposition from local populations and environmental groups. But even if such sites were ultimately built, their capacity would be enough to take care of only a small fraction of the waste accumulated over many decades. How strong is the nuclear safety regulation in Russia? What have been post-Fukushima changes? Unfortunately, it’s far from strong. In 1990s we had special safety regulator, Gosatomnadzor (or GAN). It was reporting directly to the president of country and was able to confront Rosatom on the most important safety issues. I mean there is certain difference in mandates of operator and regulator, and they must be in confrontation to improve the safety. When regulator becomes a friend to operator we are getting into Japanese situation which in the end bring us to another Fukushima sort of disaster. But that’s not the way it went in Russia. Rosatom successfully lobbied for dissolving of independent GAN. And finally it became just the department inside of another bigger structure, without any ability to control. After Fukushima, regulator proposed to close several old reactors down but that was easily ignored by Rosatom who said Russian reactors are best in the world and Fukushima would never happen in Russia. Something like that was said by Western industry after Chernobyl and all wanted to believe in it until Western-designed Fukushima exploded several times. The Russian nuclear giant, Atomsroyeport, has been clearly unwilling to abide by the Indian liability law which has a clause on supliers liability in case of an accident. What does it say on their claims of safety? It just confirms old fact that there is no 100% safe reactors. Which means, sooner or later, new Chernobyl or new Fukushima (or both) will happen again somewhere in the world. Russian industry knows very well that their reactors have vulnerabilities. And they don’t want to pay in case of another Chernobyl which they know is possible. Just like the owner of Fukushima is not paying to Japanese people……….http://www.dianuke.org/russian-reactors-are-unsafe-and-unreliable-india-shouldnt-buy-them-russian-environmentalist-vladimir-slivyak/
